modelLimits: Bottle example is physical gas-liquid exchange CO2(g) to CO2(aq), not conversion into a different substance. The short chemical bridge explicitly distinguishes reversible chemical reactions.
Real drinks also involve water vapour and acid-base equilibria. Omit these additional mechanisms without denying them. Application explicitly tracks only interface transfer in a simplified model.
CO2 glyphs are magnified representatives, not measured sizes or actual concentrations. Label application data as a molecule-tracking model, not an experiment on a real bottle.
Rates balance on average. Do not imply exact simultaneous paired swaps or a single required molecular path.
Closed does not mean insulated. Closure retains matter but does not alone establish equilibrium. Constant appearance alone does not prove exchange.
Explain net CO2 loss for this just-opened bottle. Do not assert that every open system must change or that reverse dissolution becomes zero.
Static mechanical example concerns the whole book and balanced forces, not motionless particles or a completed chemical reaction.

scenes.heading: A sealed drink looks steady. What still moves?
scenes.narration: Look at this sealed sparkling drink. There is liquid below and a space containing gas above it. The bottle has been left at the same temperature long enough to settle. It can look unchanged, even though carbon dioxide is still moving between those two places. Let us look inside and follow what the molecules do.

scenes.heading: Carbon dioxide moves both ways
scenes.narration: Some carbon dioxide is dissolved in the drink. Dissolved means it is mixed through the liquid, rather than sitting in a visible bubble. A carbon dioxide molecule can leave the liquid and enter the gas above it. A molecule from the gas can also enter the liquid and dissolve. These are opposite processes. The same kind of molecule moves between liquid and gas; it does not turn into a different substance in this example.

visual.need: Same bottle and surface inset. Actual CO2 glyphs follow continuous bidirectional crossing paths. Dissolved glyphs throughout liquid, not only bubbles. Two stable direction labels. Do not vanish into abstract groups.

Opposite processes: retain both paths and continue unpaired motion.

scenes.heading: What leaves is replaced
scenes.narration: Now watch the amount of carbon dioxide dissolved in the drink. A molecule leaving reduces that amount. A molecule entering adds to it. At equilibrium, molecules enter just as quickly as they leave, on average. So the amount dissolved does not keep rising or falling. The gas above the drink stays steady too, because each place receives carbon dioxide as quickly as it loses it. The molecules keep moving. It is the balance of the two processes that keeps the amounts steady.

scenes.heading: Dynamic equilibrium
scenes.narration: We call this dynamic equilibrium. Dynamic means the opposing processes continue. Equilibrium means their effects balance, so there is no overall change under these conditions. A rate tells us how much happens in a given time. Here, the rate of carbon dioxide leaving the liquid matches the rate entering it. Both rates are greater than zero. Think of two-way traffic: the same rate, but possibly different amounts on each side. We are matching movement per second, not sharing the molecules into two equal piles.

scenes.heading: Still object, continuing processes
scenes.narration: Compare that with a book resting on a table. The table supports the book, and the forces on it balance. The whole book stays at rest. This is static mechanical equilibrium. It does not mean the particles inside the book stop moving. Return to our drink: carbon dioxide continues crossing between liquid and gas. Here the molecules change location, not substance. In the next lesson, we will apply this idea of continuing opposing processes to a reversible chemical reaction, where reactants become products and products become reactants.

scenes.heading: The cap keeps carbon dioxide inside
scenes.narration: The cap matters because it keeps carbon dioxide inside the bottle. We call that a closed system: matter cannot enter or leave. Heat can still pass through the bottle, so closed does not mean insulated. In our example, the temperature stays constant. Now open the cap. Carbon dioxide escapes from the space above the drink into the much larger room. There is then less carbon dioxide above the liquid available to enter it. The rate returning to the liquid falls below the rate leaving. Some gas still dissolves back in, but it no longer replaces all that leaves. So the drink loses dissolved carbon dioxide overall. This is an open system because matter can cross its boundary.

scenes.heading: How much returned to the liquid?
scenes.narration: Try a new record from our sealed-bottle model. We track only carbon dioxide moving between liquid and gas. The temperature and both region volumes stay constant, and no carbon dioxide enters or leaves the bottle. In each of several ten-second intervals, sixty molecules leave the liquid. The liquid starts and ends every interval with one hundred and twenty tracked molecules. How many molecules must have entered the liquid in each interval? Explain your answer, then decide whether this record shows that exchange has stopped or is continuing in balance. Pause if you would like longer.

scenes.heading: Sixty left. Sixty returned.
scenes.narration: If sixty molecules left and none came back, the liquid would lose sixty molecules. But its tracked amount has not changed. So sixty must have entered during that same interval, replacing the sixty that left. This happens in each interval in the record. Both directions are continuing, and their average rates match: sixty molecules in ten seconds each way. That is balanced exchange, not stopped exchange. Notice that we worked out the return from the amount balance. We did not assume the two places contained equal numbers of molecules.

scenes.heading: Steady amounts, continuing exchange
scenes.narration: So, what still moves in our steady-looking sealed drink? Carbon dioxide keeps moving out of the liquid and back into it. At dynamic equilibrium, the opposing rates match on average, keeping the amounts steady under unchanged conditions. A steady appearance on its own would not tell us all of that. Our model shows the continuing exchange that explains it. Next, we will follow a reversible chemical reaction before equilibrium and see how its two rates come to match. Here are the key notes. Pause if you would like time to copy them.

scenes.heading: Key notes: what to write in your book
notes: Dynamic equilibrium: opposing processes continue at equal, non-zero average rates.
Amounts stay steady under unchanged conditions. They do not have to be equal.
Closed system: matter cannot enter or leave. Open system: matter can cross the boundary.
Static mechanical equilibrium: a whole object stays at rest with balanced forces.
